blogs.title: Propensity Evidence and the Felon‑in‑Possession Statute: Why Cutbank’s Appeal Misses the Mark
blogs.description: This post dissectes the appellate court’s affirmation that prior observations of Cutbank with the sawed‑off rifle were admissible as intrinsic evidence. It explores the line between Rule 404(b) propensity limits and the need to prove continuous possession in firearm cases, compares the Cutbank reasoning to the Ninth Circuit’s recent “Battle” line of cases, and assesses the broader implications for prosecutors’ ability to introduce prior possession evidence in § 922(g) prosecutions.

blogs.title: The Fourth‑Level Enhancement Under USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B): A Proper Fit With § 3553(a) or an Overreach?
blogs.description: An in‑depth look at the sentencing enhancement that added four levels for possessing a firearm in connection with another felony. The article evaluates the statutory text, the Sentencing Guidelines commentary, and the appellate court’s deference standard, then weighs whether the enhancement truly serves the statutory purposes of deterrence, retribution, and rehabilitation or whether it risks inflating sentences beyond what § 3553(a) mandates.

blogs.title: Harmless Error Doctrine in Federal Criminal Trials: Lessons From Cutbank’s Evidentiary Rulings
blogs.description: This entry analyzes how the Eighth Circuit applied the harmless error standard to a raft of evidentiary objections raised by Cutbank. It outlines the threshold for “substantial prejudice,” the role of cumulative error analysis, and contrasts the court’s approach with other circuits’ more rigorous harmless‑error scrutiny in high‑stakes firearms cases.

blogs.title: Armed Career Criminal Act Enhancements vs. Guideline Calculations: Reconciling Overlapping Penalties
blogs.description: The piece examines the interaction between the ACCA’s mandatory 15‑year minimum and the United States Sentencing Guidelines’ enhancement scheme, using Cutbank’s case to illustrate how courts determine which offense level “wins” when both apply. It explores the policy tensions, prior appellate guidance, and potential reforms to avoid double counting of violent felony conduct.
